doc.title: Marty Grosz interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 4, 1995

title: Touring Europe and Japan; subsidized jazz in Germany
summary: He contrasts years stuck in a Chicago saloon with later tours since 1975, and describes European department store and town subsidies for jazz.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Now you, from telling me your schedule, are quite a globe trotter. I mean this music has gotten you around to some different places. What is the European thing for this music?

Listen, if I could have done, when I was twenty-five, twenty-six, seven years old and I was working in a saloon in Chicago, six nights a week for five years and I said I’m buried, I’m forgotten, they’ll never know who I am, help, help, I’m drowning. And I would have gladly given a toe or allowed myself to be horsewhipped to go on the road, you know, to go places. To go to England. To go to Japan. To go here, to go there. And the opportunity didn’t really occur until I got to New York in ‘75, back to New York, and then three months later I’m with Dick Hyman doing a tour you know, and stuff like that. And the point is that in America jazz is dying on the vine largely, I mean as far as it being a viable, popular music, it’s become an art music. It’s not played hardly in saloons anymore. It’s not played in dance halls, it’s played on stages, concert stages. And the thing about Europe is, England has a lot of places where they like jazz. And Germany and France and then Japan. We’re going to Japan, I’ve been there about four times. I’m going

again next May. And Scandinavia and stuff like that. And they seem to think it’s a big deal. They have work. They use it, as I was telling you, they use it sort of, which is okay, they use it as accompaniment to store features. And in Germany they have these department stores that they are allowed to take a certain deduction, amount of their taxes, in fact they’re supposed to, to support the arts. It would be a great thing in this country but, try to get old Jesse and those guys convinced of it. Fat chance. And so sometimes they take it and the townships in Germany, this may be changing of course as the economics change, have like cultural programs that are subsidized. Like at the village theater there’ll be like one week there’ll be a ballet troupe, the next week a poetry reading, the next week a jazz group, the next week a string quartet. That kind of thing. But it’s subsidized. So that’s, when people book you over there for a tour, they often take advantage of that. And I went over there once with, we did some of those with Yank Lawson and Haggart and those guys and did a bunch of those. And they treated us well. Young people came. It was like a cultural event, not just a jazz event where they say well, you know, they’re playing that old stuff, we don’t, it ain’t rock so we’re not interested. Like this is culture. It was just like next week they’re doing Ibsen and this week they’re having American jazz musicians, and it’s good for you, sort of thing. And the department stores subsidize tours. I know guys, I’ve done it myself, go over and they finance the gigs by a band. You play for like a two hour concert after working hours sort of, or Thursday nights or something when they’re open late. Right in the middle of the store. Banks subsidize that and stuff. You know it’s sort of like good will and cultural. It’s like when I do in Princeton once in a while, they have Palmer Square in the middle of Princeton, they have like in the fall always a day where they, couple of days, a weekend where they have stuff. You know, “Come down, shop downtown and see what we got.” You know, this will get them downtown and they’ll buy something, and they’ll think it is, which it is, much nicer than the miracle mile outside of town with the WalMart.
